slides.title: Model Compression Pipeline: From Bloated to Blazing Fast
slides.notes: Welcome everyone. Today we're going to talk about model compression, a critical step in deploying machine learning models to real-world applications.

slides.title: Agenda
points: The 'Why': The Need for Model Optimization
The 'What': Project Overview & Baseline
The 'How': Compression Techniques Explored
The 'Wow': Building a Multi-Stage Pipeline
The 'Show': Results & Deployment
The 'Next': Conclusion & Future Work

slides.title: The Need for Speed: Why Model Optimization Matters
points: Deep learning models are growing larger and more complex.
Edge devices (like IoT and mobile) have limited resources (CPU, memory, power).
Cloud deployment costs are driven by model size and inference time.
Faster inference leads to better user experience.

slides.title: What is Model Compression?
points: A set of techniques to reduce the size and computational cost of a model.
Goal: Minimize loss in accuracy while maximizing performance gains.
Key trade-off: Size vs. Accuracy vs. Latency.

slides.title: Key Techniques in Model Compression
points: Pruning: Removing redundant model parameters.
Quantization: Reducing the precision of model weights.
Knowledge Distillation: Training a smaller 'student' model to mimic a larger 'teacher' model.
Graph Optimization: Fusing layers and removing unused operations.

slides.title: The Udacity Model Optimization Project
points: A hands-on assignment to apply model compression techniques.
Goal: Optimize a pre-trained model for a 'smart home' application.
Focus: Practical application and building an end-to-end pipeline.

slides.title: Project Goals & Objectives
points: Establish a baseline for model performance and size.
Apply at least two compression techniques.
Create a multi-stage compression pipeline.
Deploy the final, optimized model.
Compare the performance of the baseline and final models.

slides.title: The Dataset: Household Objects
points: A custom dataset of images of common household items.
Classes: bed, chair, clock, couch, keyboard, lamp, table, telephone, television, wardrobe.
A real-world dataset that presents interesting challenges.

slides.title: The Baseline Model: MobileNetV2
points: A popular, efficient convolutional neural network architecture.
Designed for mobile and resource-constrained environments.
Our starting point for optimization.
We will measure its accuracy, size, and latency.

slides.title: Post-Training Optimization: The 'Low-Hanging Fruit'
points: Techniques applied after the model has been trained.
No re-training required, making them fast to implement.
A great first step in the optimization process.

slides.title: Technique 1: Graph Optimization
points: Analyzes the model's computational graph.
Fuses layers (e.g., Conv + BatchNorm + ReLU).
Removes redundant or unused operations.
Improves inference speed without affecting accuracy.

slides.title: Graph Optimization: How it Works
slides.notes: A visual representation of how graph optimization can simplify the model's structure.

slides.title: Technique 2: Post-Training Pruning
points: Removing weights or connections that have little impact on the model's output.
Structured vs. Unstructured Pruning.
We used unstructured pruning to remove individual weights.

slides.title: Pruning: How it Works
slides.notes: A diagram showing how pruning removes connections from a neural network.

slides.title: Our Pruning Strategy
points: We used a magnitude-based pruning approach.
Weights with the smallest absolute values were removed.
We experimented with different sparsity levels to find the right balance.

slides.title: Technique 3: Post-Training Quantization
points: Reducing the numerical precision of the model's weights and activations.
Typically from 32-bit floating point (FP32) to 8-bit integer (INT8).
Leads to significant reduction in model size and faster inference.

slides.title: Quantization: How it Works
slides.notes: A visual explanation of how quantization maps a wide range of floating-point values to a smaller set of integer values.

slides.title: Our Quantization Strategy
points: We used dynamic post-training quantization.
The quantization parameters are calculated on-the-fly.
Easy to implement and provides good results.

slides.title: Post-Training Results: A Quick Win
points: We saw a significant reduction in model size.
Latency was also improved.
However, there was a noticeable drop in accuracy.

slides.title: Challenges with Post-Training Methods
points: Accuracy can suffer, especially with aggressive optimization.
Limited in the amount of compression that can be achieved.
This is where in-training optimization comes in.

slides.title: In-Training Optimization: Squeezing for More Performance
points: Integrating compression techniques into the training process.
Allows the model to adapt to the changes, preserving accuracy.
More complex and time-consuming, but more powerful.

slides.title: Technique 4: Quantization-Aware Training (QAT)
points: Simulates the effects of quantization during training.
The model learns to be robust to the reduced precision.
Results in higher accuracy than post-training quantization.

slides.title: QAT: How it Works
points: Fake quantization nodes are inserted into the model graph.
These nodes simulate the quantization and de-quantization process.
The model's weights are adjusted to minimize the quantization error.

slides.title: Technique 5: Pruning-in-Training
points: Gradually removing weights during the training process.
Allows the model to recover from the removal of connections.
Can achieve higher levels of sparsity with less accuracy loss.

slides.title: Pruning-in-Training: How it Works
points: A pruning schedule is defined (e.g., start pruning at epoch X).
The model is fine-tuned after each pruning step.
This helps the remaining weights to compensate for the removed ones.

slides.title: Technique 6: Knowledge Distillation
points: A powerful technique for model compression and transfer learning.
A smaller 'student' model is trained to mimic a larger 'teacher' model.
The student learns from the teacher's 'soft labels' (class probabilities).

slides.title: Knowledge Distillation: Teacher-Student Paradigm
slides.notes: A diagram illustrating the teacher-student relationship in knowledge distillation.

slides.title: Our Teacher and Student Models
points: Teacher: The original, un-optimized MobileNetV2 model.
Student: A smaller, compressed version of the MobileNetV2 model.
The student learns to generalize better by mimicking the teacher.

slides.title: Building the Multi-Stage Compression Pipeline
points: Combining multiple techniques to achieve maximum compression.
The output of one stage becomes the input to the next.
Our pipeline consists of three stages.

slides.title: Pipeline Stage 1: Pruning
points: We start by pruning the model to the desired sparsity.
This creates a smaller, more compact model to work with.

slides.title: Pipeline Stage 2: Quantization-Aware Training
points: We then apply QAT to the pruned model.
This further reduces the model size and improves latency.
The model is fine-tuned to recover any accuracy lost during pruning.

slides.title: Pipeline Stage 3: Knowledge Distillation
points: Finally, we use knowledge distillation to further boost the accuracy.
The pruned and quantized model acts as the student.
The original baseline model is the teacher.

slides.title: The Final Compressed Model
points: The output of our pipeline is a highly optimized model.
It is significantly smaller and faster than the baseline.
And it maintains a high level of accuracy.

slides.title: Deploying the Optimized Model
points: The final step is to deploy our model to a production environment.
We chose to deploy it as a web service on Google Cloud Run.
This allows us to easily access the model via a REST API.

slides.title: Deployment on Google Cloud Run
points: We containerized our application using Docker.
The container includes the model and a simple Flask API.
We then deployed the container to Cloud Run, which handles scaling automatically.

slides.title: Final Results: Baseline vs. Compressed
points: A final, comprehensive comparison of the two models.
Highlighting the massive improvements in size and latency.
While maintaining a very respectable accuracy.

slides.title: Key Learnings & Takeaways
points: Model optimization is a crucial skill for any machine learning engineer.
There is a clear trade-off between model size, latency, and accuracy.
A multi-stage pipeline can achieve better results than any single technique.
Post-training methods are fast, but in-training methods are more powerful.

slides.title: Future Work & Possible Improvements
points: Explore other compression techniques like tensor decomposition.
Experiment with different model architectures.
Automate the hyperparameter tuning for the compression pipeline.
Deploy the model to an actual edge device (e.g., Raspberry Pi).
